tagline: Japan's island-resort capital — 9.66M visitors a year, a national-park reef archipelago 17 nm off the capital's pier, and a resort coast with no water transit.
summary: Okinawa's main island is the engine of Japan's tropical tourism economy: Naha as the gateway, the Onna-son resort strip up the west coast, Motobu and the Churaumi Aquarium in the north — and the Kerama Islands' protected coral reefs just 15–25 nm off Naha's Tomari Pier. The prefecture drew 9.66 million visitors in 2024, yet beyond the Kerama ferries virtually everything moves on one congested coastal highway. Clean, quiet foiling networks fit both halves of the geography: zero-emission crossings into the Kerama Shoto National Park, and a west-coast resort corridor that bypasses Route 58 entirely.

demand_signals.label: Okinawa visitor arrivals
demand_signals.note: Third-highest on record, ~95% of pre-pandemic peak; diving, beach-resort and island-hopping tourism led the recovery.

demand_signals.label: Kerama high-speed ferry ridership
demand_signals.value: Daily fast-ferry rotations, routinely sold out in season
demand_signals.note: Marine Liner Tokashiki (~35 min) and Queen Zamami (~50–70 min) run high-speed diesel services from Tomari to Tokashiki and Zamami — a proven, capacity-constrained fast-boat market into a national park.

demand_signals.label: Protected reef waters
demand_signals.note: Japan's 31st national park — designated for its coral reefs and humpback whale wintering grounds. Diesel fast ferries serve it today; a zero-emission fleet is the conservation-aligned upgrade.

demand_signals.label: One-road resort coast
demand_signals.value: Naha ↔ Onna-son ~1.5–2h by Route 58 in season
demand_signals.note: The west-coast resort strip (Renaissance, Halekulani, ANA InterContinental Manza, Hoshinoya) has no water transit; peak-season highway congestion is the standing arrival pain for every resort north of the airport.

use_cases.title: Zero-emission Kerama crossings
use_cases.body: Clean, near-silent foiling service from Naha/Tomari to Tokashiki (~17 nm) and Zamami (~20 nm) — modernising an adopted fast-ferry habit with zero-emission entry into the national park's reef and whale waters.

use_cases.title: West-coast resort corridor
use_cases.body: A scheduled water shuttle from Naha up the resort strip — Chatan/American Village, Yomitan, Onna-son, Motobu (~29 nm) — bypassing Route 58 congestion and delivering guests to resort jetties; N35 Shuttle-class capacity fits the arrival flows.

use_cases.title: Resort-jetty private transfers
use_cases.body: Direct foiling transfers between Naha, the Onna-son luxury cluster (Halekulani, Hoshinoya, ANA IC Manza) and Motobu/Sesoko — replacing car-plus-highway chains with one smooth hop along the reef coast.

use_cases.title: Inter-archipelago line-hauls
use_cases.body: Naha ↔ Miyako (~155 nm) and Naha ↔ Ishigaki (~220 nm) are flown today — hybrid foiling line-hauls add a premium surface option across the prefecture's open-ocean spine with no charging-infrastructure dependency.

journeys.today: A high-speed diesel ferry (~35 min) on a fixed timetable, often fully booked in season and weather-cancelled on exposed days — running diesel into a protected reef park.
journeys.with_navier: A smooth, zero-emission foiling crossing that flies above the chop, adds frequency the villages can't, and enters the national park clean and near-silent.

journeys.today: 60–120 minutes up congested Route 58 by car or limousine bus — the standard arrival experience for the island's premium resorts.
journeys.with_navier: A ~20 nm foiling glide up the reef coast straight to the resort jetty — the arrival becomes part of the holiday.

journeys.today: ~2 hours by road from the Churaumi Aquarium corner of the island; no scheduled water link.
journeys.with_navier: A ~29 nm coastal foiling run connecting the island's two tourism poles in under an hour on the water.

journeys.today: Air-only — the ~155 nm open-ocean leg has no passenger surface option at all.
journeys.with_navier: A Quanta-LR hybrid line-haul opens a premium sea connection across the prefecture's spine, no charging stop required.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Two all-electric meshes: the Kerama crossings from Naha/Tomari (Tokashiki ~17 nm, Zamami ~20 nm) and the west-coast resort corridor (Chatan ~10 nm, Onna-son ~20 nm, Motobu ~29 nm) — all deep inside the 70 nm envelope, on a main island with strong grid capacity.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The prefecture's open-ocean spine is explicit hybrid territory: Naha ↔ Miyako (~155 nm) and Naha ↔ Ishigaki (~220 nm) are flown today and far beyond all-electric range — never imply one continuous electric network. Quanta-LR adds these line-hauls with zero charging-infrastructure dependency on the outer islands.

competitive_landscape: The Kerama Islands are served by village-operated fast and car ferries from Tomari (Marine Liner Tokashiki, Queen Zamami, Ferry Zamami) — high-frequency, seasonal sell-outs, and weather-fragile: textbook demand evidence for a faster, smoother, cleaner replacement tier. On the main island itself the incumbent is the highway: resort access runs on Route 58 and limousine buses, with no scheduled coastal water service at all. Between islands, JTA and Ryukyu Air Commuter carry the Naha↔Miyako/Ishigaki flows by air. A mature, growing 9.66M-visitor market with water on three sides and almost no modern water mobility is the opportunity.

precedents.why_it_matters: The two-platform island-network playbook — short electric meshes plus long hybrid spines — proven at national scale; directly analogous to Okinawa's geometry.

seasonality: Typhoon season (Jun–Oct) is more severe than mainland Japan and the NE winter monsoon (Nov–Mar) brings sustained chop to the Kerama crossings — the two windows that drive today's ferry cancellations. Foiling above the sea state converts that weather-fragility into a reliability premium, and the Dec–Apr humpback whale season in the Keramas rewards quiet, low-wake operation. Late spring and autumn are the calm peaks.
regulatory_note: Operations sit under the Japan Coast Guard 11th Regional HQ (Naha), MLIT Kyushu oversight, and Naha Port Authority / Okinawa Prefecture pier jurisdiction. Kerama Shoto National Park (2014) gives clean-fleet operation a concrete conservation mandate — displacing diesel in reef and whale-wintering waters — aligned with Japan's 2050 carbon-neutrality target and MLIT zero-emission-vessel programmes. Quiet, safe-distance operation around wintering humpbacks is both a permit advantage and a brand asset.
